title: Why Consistency Compounds
summary: One test, one note, one clearer name a day looks like nothing. A few months later it adds up. What habit research says about consistency, and how to keep it going.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Most mornings the desk looks the same: a notebook by the keyboard, a coffee going cold, one more card added to a row of half-finished ideas. From the outside, nothing is happening. No launch, no breakthrough, nobody clapping. Just someone coming back to work that still needs time.

Consistency is unimpressive while it's happening. One page read, one test added, one awkward conversation patched up, one workout with no story attached. Any single day is too small to show anyone. Over a few months, the traces get hard to ignore. The rest of this post looks at how that compounding actually works, what habit research says about the slow middle part, and how to keep a practice alive when the week goes sideways.

Compounding is mostly less friction

There's no magic in it. Each repetition makes the next one a little cheaper. A note you take today is context next month. A test you add before a refactor is the reason you dare to refactor later. A small promise you keep to yourself makes the next one feel less theoretical. The gain builds up inside the system long before it shows up as a result.

Code works the same way. Martin Fowler describes refactoring as something you do continuously, "as regular and indivisible a part of programming as typing if statements" (Opportunistic Refactoring). The habit is often summed up as the camp site rule: always leave the code in a better state than you found it. A team that works like this, he writes, should hardly ever need to plan a refactoring, because the cleanup happens as a constant stream of small adjustments. Rename one confusing concept every time you touch it, and six months later the module reads like a different codebase.

What the habit research says

The study people cite most here comes from Phillippa Lally and colleagues at UCL. They asked 96 volunteers to pick one eating, drinking or exercise behavior and repeat it daily in the same context, like "after breakfast", for 84 days, rating how automatic it felt along the way. As the BPS Research Digest reports, the average time to reach peak automaticity was 66 days, and the spread was huge: from 18 days to a predicted 254 (How to form a habit). People who chose exercise took about one and a half times as long as people who chose eating or drinking habits.

Two findings are useful for everyday life. First, the curve is slow. If a new habit still feels like effort in week three, that's normal, and it doesn't mean the habit is failing. Second, a single missed day had little impact on later progress. Missing many days did add up and lowered how automatic the behavior became. So skip the guilt over one lost day, and don't let it stretch into a week.

The first evidence is small

That slow curve is why consistency is hard to judge early. You want proof that the effort is working, and the first proof is usually just less resistance. You open the project faster. You recover from a mistake with less drama. You ask for help sooner. You spot a familiar trap before you're fully in it. None of that looks like a result, yet each one nudges a lot of future choices.

Small practices survive busy weeks

Big declarations feel great on day one. "New year, new me" turns daily life into a stage, and most people can't stay on a stage for long. A smaller practice fits inside ordinary days. It survives a hectic sprint, a tired evening, a month where progress looks plain. Fifteen minutes of reading the codebase every morning will take you further than one heroic weekend you never repeat.

Consistency still needs steering. Repeating something that stopped helping a while ago is stubbornness. The point is to keep coming back with enough attention to notice what to keep, what to change and what to drop.

Most visible skills started small

A lot of what looks like talent is consistency that finally became visible. The teammate who stays composed in a hard meeting practiced many small pauses before speaking. The engineer who reads a codebase fast spent many mornings tracing behavior nobody saw. The writer with clear sentences deleted plenty of unclear ones in private. (A sibling post, why preparation often looks invisible, picks up that thread.)

Try this week

  • Pick one practice small enough for your worst day: one test, one note, one clearer name.
  • Attach it to something you already do, like opening your laptop or merging a PR.
  • If you miss a day, pick it up the next day and move on.
  • After a month, write down one thing that got easier. That's your early evidence.

faqs.q: How long does it take to form a habit?
faqs.a: In a UCL study led by Phillippa Lally, 96 volunteers repeated one daily behavior for 84 days. The average time to reach peak automaticity was 66 days, ranging from 18 days to a predicted 254. Exercise habits took about one and a half times as long as eating or drinking habits.

faqs.q: Does missing a day ruin a new habit?
faqs.a: No. In the same study, a single missed day had little impact on later progress. Missing many days did add up and lowered how automatic the habit became, so pick it up the next day and keep going.

faqs.q: What does consistency look like in a codebase?
faqs.a: Small improvements every time you touch the code. Martin Fowler calls it opportunistic refactoring, often summed up as the camp site rule: leave the code better than you found it. Teams that work this way rarely need to plan a separate refactoring.
